opus-5.5.text:
I'd say I'm not super confident about it, but I think there are a few reasons that push me in that direction. One is just that war is really costly. When you have two actors who are in conflict, there's almost always some bargain that both of them would prefer to actually fighting it out, because fighting destroys a lot of value. Historically the reasons we haven't reached those bargains are things like being unable to commit credibly, being uncertain about each other's strength, or having leaders whose interests diverge from their populations'. And I think a lot of those frictions look like the kinds of things that get easier to solve as the world becomes richer, more interconnected, and as we get better tools for verification and coordination.

I think AI in particular could make a big difference there. If you have systems that can help monitor agreements, verify what the other side is doing, help negotiate, and generally reduce the information problems that lead to conflict, then a lot of the classic causes of war get weaker. And then there's the trend line: if you look over the last few centuries, the fraction of people dying in wars has gone down, even if it's noisy and there are horrifying exceptions. As the stakes of war get higher, especially with more destructive technology, the incentive to build institutions that prevent it also goes up.

So my expectation is that in the long run, if things go reasonably well, we end up in a world where large-scale violent conflict is pretty rare, more like the way disputes inside a stable country get resolved through courts than the way states fought historically. But I want to stress that the transition is the dangerous part. The period where we're developing very powerful technology, particularly AI, before we've built the institutions to manage it, is exactly when the risk of catastrophic conflict could be highest. So "eventually low" doesn't mean "low along the way."

r001.rationale: The response explains that war destroys value and that institutions, verification, and coordination can help actors resolve conflicts through bargains instead of fighting.

r002.rationale: It says AI could monitor agreements, verify actions, and help negotiate, but does not communicate that AI speeds up the cognitive work of discovering how society should be organized to reduce war.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic picture is that war is mostly a mistake, in the sense that it's negative-sum. If two parties fight, they're both spending resources destroying things, and almost always there's some deal they could have struck instead where both of them end up better off than the expected outcome of fighting. So the question is really why that deal doesn't get struck, and the standard answers are things like: the parties can't credibly commit to the terms, or they have private information and can't agree on what the outcome of the war would be, or there's just some irrationality or value disagreement that makes negotiation hard.

My expectation is that most of those obstacles get a lot smaller over time. As institutions and technology improve, it becomes easier to make credible commitments, easier to verify what the other side is doing, easier to agree on what would actually happen if you fought, so you can just skip the fighting and go to the settlement. And as people get wealthier and more capable, the relative cost of war goes up. You have more to lose, and you have better options for getting what you want without it. So I'd expect war to become rarer in the same way that, say, duels became rarer. Not because people stopped disagreeing, but because the mechanism became obviously dumb relative to the alternatives.

I want to be careful here, because I don't think that's inevitable or that the transition is smooth. There are periods, especially around big technological changes, where things could get a lot worse before they get better. If one party gets a decisive advantage for a while, or if the balance of offense and defense shifts suddenly, that's exactly when you'd expect the normal logic to break down. So when I say "eventually," I mean something like: conditional on getting through those transitions without a catastrophe, I think the long-run equilibrium is one where organized violence is very rare, because sufficiently sophisticated agents just don't find it worthwhile. It's more of a statement about where things settle than a prediction that the next century will be peaceful.

r001.rationale: The response frames war as a costly way to resolve conflicts and describes institutions and technology making peaceful settlements easier to reach and enforce.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI or suggest that it could accelerate this progress by speeding up the work of discovering how to organize society.

astra-6.text:
I think a basic reason is that war is costly. If two parties fight, they generally both prefer some negotiated outcome to actually paying the costs of fighting. The hard part is finding an agreement they can both trust, especially when their relative power is changing.

That doesn’t mean you can just point out that war is inefficient and everyone stops. You have problems where people disagree about who would win, or where one side can’t credibly promise not to exploit the other later. Those are real obstacles. But they seem like problems that better institutions, better information, and better mechanisms for making commitments can make progress on.

So my expectation isn’t primarily that people become much nicer. It’s that there’s a large surplus available from avoiding war, and over time people have incentives to find ways to capture that surplus. I wouldn’t regard that as inevitable, or expect a smooth decline in conflict. But over a sufficiently long period, I’d expect us to get substantially better at resolving disputes without destroying things both sides value.

r001.rationale: The response describes finding better institutions, information, and commitment mechanisms to resolve disputes without the costs and losses of war.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI or suggest it could speed the work of discovering how to organize society to reduce war.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that war is costly, and there’s usually some deal that would leave both sides better off than fighting. The hard part is finding that deal and making it credible. You might disagree about who would win, or you might worry that if you make concessions today, the other side will be in a stronger position to demand more tomorrow.

Those are real problems, but they don’t seem like immutable features of the world. You can have better information, better mechanisms for making commitments, and institutions that make aggression less attractive. And as societies get richer, there’s more value in preserving what you have relative to what you can gain by taking someone else’s territory.

I wouldn’t expect that to happen smoothly or inevitably. But over a sufficiently long period, I expect people to find ways to capture more of the gains from avoiding war. It’s a bit like asking why we don’t expect disputes between individuals to keep being settled by violence at the same rate forever. There’s a large incentive to build arrangements that let people resolve those disputes more cheaply.

r001.rationale: It describes reducing war as finding better information, credible commitments, and institutions to resolve conflicts and avoid the costs of fighting.

r002.rationale: It discusses mechanisms for reducing war but does not mention AI or say that AI could speed the cognitive work of discovering those mechanisms.
